title: Akple (Ewe maize and cassava dough dumpling)

ingredients.name: fine white cornmeal (or fermented corn dough)

steps: Mix the cornmeal and cassava flour with 400 ml of the water to a smooth paste and let it rest for 30 minutes.
Bring the remaining 400 ml of water and the salt to a boil in a heavy pot, then reduce the heat to medium.
Pour in the paste in a steady stream, stirring all the time with a wooden spoon so lumps do not form.
Keep stirring and pressing the mixture against the side of the pot until it forms a thick, stiff dough, about 10 minutes. Akple is firmer and drier than banku.
Cover and cook on low heat for 5 minutes to steam, then stir hard once more until the dough is smooth and pulls away from the pot.
Shape into smooth balls using a wet bowl or ladle. Serve warm with okra soup or fish stew.

title: Aprapransa (Ga roasted corn flour with palm nut soup and fish)

ingredients.name: roasted cornmeal (or plain cornmeal toasted in a dry pan until golden)

steps: If your cornmeal is not already roasted, toast it in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring constantly, for about 8 minutes until it smells nutty and turns light brown.
Put the palm nut cream, onion, tomatoes, whole scotch bonnet, ginger and 400 ml of the water in a pot and simmer for 20 minutes.
Add the flaked smoked fish and salt and cook for another 10 minutes. Remove the scotch bonnet, or mash it into the soup if you like more heat.
In a small bowl, loosen the roasted cornmeal with the remaining water to avoid lumps, then pour it slowly into the simmering soup, stirring constantly.
Cook on low heat for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring, until the mixture thickens to a soft porridge-like consistency.
Serve hot, topped with halved boiled eggs.

title: Banku (Ghanaian fermented corn and cassava dumpling)

ingredients.name: fine white cornmeal (or ready-made fermented corn dough from an African grocer)
plain yoghurt or lime juice, for a little tang if the dough is not already fermented

steps: Stir the cornmeal, cassava flour, yoghurt or lime juice and 300 ml of the water into a smooth, runny batter. Cover and leave it for at least 1 hour so the flavour sours slightly.
Add the salt and the remaining water to the batter and pour it into a heavy non-stick pot, whisking so no lumps form.
Set the pot over medium heat and stir constantly with a sturdy wooden spoon as the mixture thickens into a heavy, sticky paste. This takes about 10 minutes and needs strong arms.
Turn the heat very low, cover the pot and let the banku steam for 5 minutes, then beat it firmly against the side of the pot to make it smooth and elastic.
Repeat the steaming and beating once or twice more until the paste is glossy, stretchy and no longer tastes raw.
Wet a small bowl, scoop in a portion, rotate it to make a smooth ball and turn it out onto a plate. Serve hot with okra stew, light soup or pepper sauce and fried fish.

title: Bofrot (Ghanaian puff-puff fried dough balls)
steps: Whisk the flour, sugar, yeast, nutmeg and salt together in a large bowl.
Gradually stir in the warm water to make a thick, sticky batter, beating well with your hand or a spoon for a few minutes.
Cover and leave in a warm place for 1 hour until doubled and full of bubbles.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to medium heat, about 170 C.
Scoop up a handful of batter, squeeze out a ball between your thumb and finger and drop it into the oil. Fry in batches without crowding.
Turn the balls so they brown evenly, 4 to 5 minutes in total, then drain on paper towels. Serve warm.

title: Etor (Ga mashed plantain or yam with palm oil and eggs)

ingredients.name: very ripe plantains (or 600 g yam), peeled

steps: Cut the plantains or yam into chunks and boil in lightly salted water for 15 to 20 minutes until completely soft. Drain.
Mash the plantain or yam with a fork or pestle until mostly smooth but still a little rustic.
Heat the palm oil in a small pan, fry the onion for 2 minutes and mix this into the mash with the remaining salt.
Spoon the etor onto plates, shaping it into a mound, and arrange halved boiled eggs around it.
Scatter with crushed peanuts and serve warm, traditionally for celebrations and special occasions.

title: Fufu (Ghanaian pounded cassava and plantain with light soup)

ingredients.name: cassava, peeled and cut into chunks
hot water, plus more if needed

steps: Put the cassava and plantain in a pot, cover with water and boil for about 25 minutes until completely soft.
Drain, keeping a cup of the cooking water, and remove any woody core fibre from the cassava.

Pound the hot cassava and plantain in a mortar with a pestle, turning the mass between strikes, until it becomes smooth and stretchy. Alternatively blend in a powerful food processor with a little of the hot water.
If you used a processor, return the mixture to a pot over low heat and stir vigorously for 2 to 3 minutes until it forms a cohesive, elastic dough.
Wet your hands or a bowl, shape the fufu into balls and serve immediately with light soup or palm nut soup. Fufu is swallowed in small pieces rather than chewed.

title: Gari and beans (Ghanaian gob3 cassava flakes with stewed beans)
steps: Simmer the soaked beans in fresh water for 40 to 50 minutes until soft, then drain.
Heat the palm oil in a pot and fry the onion and ginger for 5 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and pepper and cook for 10 minutes into a thick sauce, then stir in the beans and salt.
Sprinkle the gari over the beans in a thin layer, pour 3 to 4 tablespoons of hot water over it and cover for 5 minutes to let it swell.
Fold the gari gently through the beans with a spoon until evenly mixed and fluffy. Serve with fried plantain.

title: Gari soaking (Ghanaian cold sweet cassava flakes with milk and peanuts)
steps: Put the gari in a large bowl.
Pour over the cold water and stir, then let it soak for 5 minutes until the flakes swell.
Stir in the sugar, evaporated milk and ginger, and taste for sweetness.
Add the ice cubes and top with peanuts. Serve immediately, while the gari still has a slight crunch.

title: Ice kenkey (Ghanaian chilled kenkey in sweet milk)
steps: Break the kenkey into pieces and mash with a fork or the back of a spoon until it is loose and crumbly.
Stir in the cold milk and condensed milk until the kenkey softens and the mixture is sweet and creamy.
Add the ginger or nutmeg and taste for sweetness.
Divide among bowls, add the ice cubes and scatter with peanuts. Serve straight away, ideally with fried dough or bread on the side.

title: Jollof rice (Ghanaian spiced tomato rice)

ingredients.name: large onion, half blended and half sliced
scotch bonnet pepper (or 1 to 2 hot chillies)

steps: Rinse the rice until the water runs nearly clear, then drain well.
Blend the tomatoes, half the onion, the scotch bonnet, ginger and garlic into a smooth purée.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot and fry the sliced onion until soft. Stir in the tomato paste and fry for 3 minutes.
Add the purée, curry powder, thyme and bay leaves and cook over medium heat for about 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce is thick and the oil rises to the top.
Pour in the stock and bring to a boil, then add the rice and salt and stir well so every grain is coated.
Cover tightly with foil under the lid, reduce the heat to very low and steam for 25 to 30 minutes without stirring until the rice is tender.
Fluff with a fork and serve with fried plantain, grilled chicken or salad.

title: Kelewele (Ghanaian spiced fried plantain)

ingredients.name: very ripe plantains (yellow with black spots)

steps: Peel the plantains and cut them into bite-sized cubes.
Mix the ginger, garlic, cayenne, cloves, salt and grated onion in a bowl, then toss the plantain cubes in this mixture.
Leave to marinate for 15 to 20 minutes so the spices cling to the fruit.
Heat the oil in a deep pan to medium-hot and fry the plantain in batches for 3 to 4 minutes until golden brown and slightly crisp at the edges.
Drain on paper towels and serve warm, traditionally with roasted peanuts, or alongside red red or fish stew.

title: Kenkey (Ghanaian steamed fermented-corn dumpling)

ingredients.name: fermented corn dough (buy ready-made from an African grocer)
dried corn husks or squares of foil (soaked husks are traditional; use banana leaf or foil as a substitute)

steps: Mix the corn dough with the salt in a bowl, then set aside about one third of it.
Boil the water in a pot, stir in the one third portion and cook over low heat for 10 minutes, stirring constantly, until it becomes a thick, translucent paste.
Let the cooked paste cool slightly, then knead it into the raw dough until evenly combined.
Divide the dough into 4 to 6 balls. Wrap each ball tightly in soaked corn husks or foil so the parcel keeps its shape while cooking.
Place the parcels in a large pot, add water to cover and simmer for 1.5 to 2 hours, topping up with hot water when needed.
Lift the kenkey out and let it cool for 10 minutes before unwrapping. Serve with shito, fried fish and sliced tomatoes and onions.

title: Koko (Ghanaian spiced millet porridge)
steps: Whisk the millet flour with 250 ml of the cold water until smooth, then leave it to sit for about 10 minutes.
Bring the remaining water to a boil in a pot with the ginger, cloves and black pepper.
Slowly whisk the millet mixture into the boiling water, stirring constantly so lumps do not form.
Turn the heat low and simmer for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring often, until thick and smooth.
Stir in the sugar and salt and pour into bowls. Add evaporated milk if you like. Serve with koose or bread.

title: Kokonte (Ghanaian brown cassava-flour swallow)

ingredients.name: kokonte flour (dried cassava flour; plain cassava flour also works)

steps: Bring 500 ml of water and a pinch of salt to a boil in a heavy saucepan.
Mix the kokonte flour with the remaining 200 ml of cold water in a bowl into a smooth slurry with no lumps.
Pour the slurry into the boiling water in a thin stream while stirring briskly with a wooden spoon.
Lower the heat and keep stirring for 8 to 10 minutes, pressing the mixture against the pot, until it is thick, dark and glossy.
Scoop with a wet spoon into serving bowls and shape into smooth balls. Eat with groundnut soup or palm nut soup.

title: Koose (Ghanaian black-eyed pea fritters)

ingredients.name: scotch bonnet pepper (or 1 to 2 hot chillies)

steps: Drain the soaked peas, rub off the skins and rinse away what floats.
Blend the peas with the onion, pepper and ginger, adding just a splash of water, into a thick, fluffy paste.
Beat the paste vigorously with a wooden spoon for 3 to 4 minutes to add air, then mix in the flour and salt.
Heat the oil to about 180 C. Drop in tablespoons of the batter and fry until deep golden brown and crisp, about 3 to 4 minutes, turning once.
Drain on paper towels and serve hot with Hausa koko, gari or bread, or on their own with pepper sauce.

title: Kyinkyinga (Ghanaian spiced peanut beef skewers)

ingredients.name: beef sirloin or rump, in thin strips
onion, cut into wedges, to serve

steps: Mix the ground peanuts with the ginger, chilli powder, paprika, onion powder, garlic powder and salt to make the dry spice rub.
Toss the beef strips with the oil and then coat generously in the spice mix. Cover and marinate for at least 1 hour.
Soak wooden skewers in water for 20 minutes to stop them burning.
Thread the meat onto the skewers, folding the strips in accordion style, and add onion wedges if you like.
Grill over hot charcoal or under a very hot grill for 8 to 10 minutes, turning, until the edges are charred and the meat is cooked through.
Dust with a little extra spice mix and serve with sliced onions and tomatoes.

title: Light soup (Ghanaian goat and tomato pepper soup)

ingredients.name: goat meat on the bone (or lamb or beef), in pieces
scotch bonnet peppers (or less, to taste)

steps: Blend one tomato, half the onion, one pepper, the ginger and garlic with a little water.
Put the meat in a pot with the blended mixture, salt and 400 ml of the water. Bring to a boil, then simmer, covered, for 40 minutes until the meat starts to soften.
Blend the remaining tomatoes and onion and add them to the pot with the tomato paste and remaining water.
Add the second pepper whole and simmer for 30 to 40 minutes more, until the meat is tender and the broth is thin, bright and aromatic.
Taste for salt and serve hot with fufu, banku or kenkey.

title: Mpoto mpoto (Ghanaian yam pottage with smoked fish)

ingredients.name: yam (or cocoyam, or white sweet potato), peeled and cubed

steps: Boil the yam in water for 20 to 25 minutes until very soft, then drain, keeping about 150 ml of the cooking liquid.
Roughly mash the yam with a fork, leaving some small chunks for texture.
Heat the palm oil in a pot, fry the onion until soft, then add the tomatoes and scotch bonnet and cook for 6 to 8 minutes into a thick sauce.
Add the flaked fish, ground shrimp if using and salt, and stir for 2 minutes.
Fold in the mashed yam and enough of the reserved liquid to make a thick, moist pottage. Simmer on low heat for 10 minutes and serve hot.

title: Nkatie cake (Ghanaian peanut brittle)
steps: Lightly grease a baking tray or a clean work surface and a rolling pin, and have a knife ready. Set the peanuts and salt in a bowl next to the stove.
Put the sugar and water in a heavy pan over medium heat. Stir only until the sugar dissolves, then stop stirring.
Cook for 6 to 8 minutes until the syrup turns a deep golden caramel. Take care, as the sugar becomes extremely hot.
Remove from the heat and quickly stir in the peanuts and salt until fully coated.
Tip the mixture onto the greased surface, roll out to about 1 cm thick and cut into bars while still warm.
Leave to cool and harden completely before breaking apart and storing in an airtight container.

title: Palaver sauce (Ghanaian kontomire greens stew with eggs and fish)

ingredients.name: spinach (or kontomire or taro leaves), washed and chopped

steps: Heat the palm oil in a wide pot and fry the onion for 5 minutes until soft.
Add the tomatoes and scotch bonnet and cook for about 10 minutes until they break down into a thick sauce.
Stir in the ground melon seeds with 100 ml of water and simmer for 5 minutes.
Add the flaked fish, ground shrimp and salt and cook for a further 5 minutes.
Add the greens in batches, stirring until wilted, and simmer for 10 minutes without a lid.
Nestle the boiled eggs in the stew, warm through and serve with boiled yam, rice or fufu.

title: Palm nut soup (Ghanaian chicken abenkwan)
steps: Season the chicken with salt, half the onion, the ginger and garlic, and leave for 20 minutes.
Place the chicken in a pot with 300 ml of the water and simmer for 15 minutes.
Add the palm nut cream, remaining water, tomatoes, the rest of the onion, whole scotch bonnet and herbs.
Simmer gently for 30 to 40 minutes, uncovered, until the soup has thickened and a layer of red oil floats on top.
Taste and adjust the salt, remove the scotch bonnet and serve with fufu, banku or rice balls.

title: Plakali (Ahanta cassava dough staple)
steps: Whisk the cassava flour with 300 ml of the water until smooth and let it sit for 20 minutes.
Bring the remaining water and salt to a boil in a heavy pot.
Reduce the heat, pour in the batter and stir continuously with a wooden spoon so lumps do not form.
Cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring and pressing against the pot, until the dough is thick, translucent and stretchy.
Shape into smooth balls with a wet bowl and serve hot with palm nut soup or groundnut soup.

source.note: Original write-up of a traditional preparation, made for World Recipes. Quantities are approximate; adjust to taste.

title: Red red (Ghanaian black-eyed pea stew with fried plantain)
steps: Drain the soaked beans, cover with fresh water and simmer for 40 to 50 minutes until completely tender. Drain, keeping a little liquid.
Heat the palm oil in a pot, add the onion and ginger and fry for 5 minutes.
Stir in the tomatoes, tomato paste and scotch bonnet and cook for 10 minutes until jammy.
Add the beans with a few tablespoons of the reserved liquid and salt, then simmer for 10 to 15 minutes so the beans take on the red colour of the oil.
Peel and slice the plantains on the diagonal and fry them in hot oil until deep golden on both sides. Drain on paper towels.
Serve the beans hot with the fried plantain, and with gari or rice if you like.

title: Shito (Ghanaian black pepper sauce)

ingredients.name: hot red chillies or 2 scotch bonnets
ground dried shrimp or crayfish powder (or dried fish powder)

steps: Blend the onion, ginger, garlic and chillies with 3 tablespoons of the oil into a coarse purée.
Heat the remaining oil in a heavy pan and add the purée carefully, as it will spit.
Fry over low to medium heat for about 30 minutes, stirring often, until the water has cooked off and the paste darkens.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 10 more minutes.
Add the ground shrimp, salt and black pepper and cook for another 10 to 15 minutes until the sauce is dark brown to black and the oil separates.
Cool completely, spoon into a clean jar and keep refrigerated. Serve with kenkey, rice, waakye or boiled yam.

title: Tubaani (Ghanaian steamed black-eyed pea pudding)

ingredients.name: chilli flakes or 1 chopped hot pepper
banana leaves, large leaves or foil, for wrapping

steps: Rub the soaked peas between your hands to loosen the skins, rinse away the skins and drain the peas.
Blend the peeled peas with the water, salt and chilli to a thick, smooth batter.
Scoop portions of about 4 tablespoons onto pieces of banana leaf, foil or baking parchment and fold into tight parcels.
Steam the parcels over simmering water in a covered pot for 45 to 50 minutes until firm.
Heat the oil in a small pan and fry the sliced onion with a pinch of chilli for 3 minutes.
Unwrap the tubaani and serve hot with the onion and pepper oil, or with a tomato stew.
